# How to Read a Media Plan Before You Approve It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-read-a-media-plan/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: A media plan says where a marketing budget will be spent, over what period, in what proportions, and what each part should produce. Before approving one, read the objective, the expected outcomes and the cost basis, check the programmatic supply path, and ask what the plan assumes, what happens when a channel fails, and who owns the data afterwards.

A media plan is the document that says where a marketing budget will be spent, over what period, in what proportions, and what each part is expected to produce. It is the point at which strategy turns into money, and it is usually approved by people who have not been told how to read one. Read three things first: the objective, the expected outcomes and the cost basis. Then check where programmatic money actually goes, since the ANA found the average campaign in its 2023 study ran on about 44,000 websites.

## What a good plan contains

**The objective, in one sentence,** stated as an outcome the company can observe: funded accounts, qualified leads, activated users, at a cost per outcome and a volume. A plan whose objective is "awareness" or "reach" should say what awareness is expected to lead to and how anyone will know. Our piece on [measuring brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/) covers what a brand objective can be measured against.

**The audience,** defined precisely enough that a channel can be chosen for it. Who, where, what they are doing when they might be reached, and what they need to believe.

**The channel mix,** listed with the share of budget for each and the reason each is there. The reason should connect to the audience and the objective, not to the channel's availability.

**The flighting:** when each channel runs, at what weight, over the plan period. A plan that spends evenly across every channel for every week has not made any decisions. It has also made the plan impossible to measure later: a [marketing mix model](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-marketing-mix-modeling/) cannot separate channels whose spend never moved.

**The expected results,** by channel: the volume of outcomes, the cost per outcome, and the assumptions behind each. Where the assumption is a guess, it should say so.

**The measurement approach:** how each channel's outcomes will be tracked, in whose systems, and how the plan will be adjusted when the numbers arrive. A plan with no holdout or test on its largest line has no way to learn whether that line worked.

**The band map,** for companies in reviewed categories: which channels are open, which require approvals the plan is not counting on, and which are closed.

## The columns and what they mean

Most plans are a table.

| Column | What it says | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Channel and placement or partner | Where the money goes | Named sellers, not "run of network" |
| Format and audience | What runs, to whom | Whether the audience can actually be targeted in this category |
| Dates and weight | Flighting | Variation that later analysis can read |
| Impressions or reach | Volume of exposure | Viewable and verified, or gross |
| Cost and cost basis (CPM, CPC, CPA) | What the channel is bought on | The conversion assumption from that unit to customers |
| Expected outcomes | The plan's promise | Where each number came from |
| Share of budget | Priorities | Whether it matches the stated reasons |
| Fees | What the partner earns | In dollars, and what makes them rise |

The two columns to interrogate are expected outcomes and the cost basis. Expected outcomes are the plan's promise; ask where each number came from. The cost basis tells you what the channel is being bought on. A channel bought on CPM with an expected number of customers attached has done a conversion calculation somewhere, and the assumptions in that calculation are the plan's real content. Our explainer on [CPM, CPC, CPA, CPL and ROAS](https://lowob.com/research/cpm-cpc-cpa-cpl-roas-explained/) covers what each basis hides.

Check what "impressions" means. The Media Rating Council's viewability standard counts a display impression as viewable when half its pixels are on screen for one second. A plan's gross impressions may be well above the viewable, human ones.

## Where programmatic money goes

Programmatic lines deserve a separate look, because the supply chain between the advertiser's money and the publisher is long. ISBA and PwC's 2020 UK study traced spend through matched supply chains and found publishers received about 51% of advertiser spend, with about 15% unattributable. The ANA's 2023 US study, covering $123 million of spend, found the average campaign ran on about 44,000 top-level domains, and made-for-advertising sites took 21% of impressions and 15% of spend. The top 500 domains had a 50% lower fraud rate than the long tail.

The ANA's recommendations translate directly into plan questions: favour inclusion lists over exclusion lists, buy the fewest properties through the most direct path, and work only with sites where viewability, fraud and brand safety can be measured.

IAB Tech Lab's supply-chain standards give a way to investigate the seller path. ads.txt lets a publisher list who is authorised to sell its inventory. sellers.json, published by each ad system, discloses the legal entity paid under each seller ID and whether it is a publisher or an intermediary. The SupplyChain object lists every node that touched a bid request. Together they let a buyer ask who is in the path and why. They do not replace independent outcome measurement. Our piece on [programmatic media numbers you can trust](https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/) covers the verification side.

> A channel bought on CPM with an expected number of customers attached has done a conversion calculation somewhere. The assumptions in that calculation are the plan's real content.

## The questions to ask before approving

1. **Which of these channels has this company, or this partner, run for this category before, and what happened?**
2. **If one channel fails in the first two weeks, where does its budget go, and who decides?**
3. **Which lines assume an approval that has not arrived?**
4. **What does the plan look like at half the budget?** The answer reveals which channels the planner actually believes in.
5. **For programmatic lines: how many domains, on an inclusion list or not, and through which sellers?**
6. **Who owns the accounts, the tracking and the data when the plan ends?**
7. **What is the fee, in dollars, and what makes it go up?** Our piece on [percent-of-spend fees](https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/) explains why this question matters.

## The plan for a company that cannot buy the usual channels

For a company the ad platforms restrict, a conventional media plan is mostly lines that will not run. The plan that works starts from the band map, allocates the first weeks to cheap measurement across the open-band channels, commits the bulk of the budget only after something reads, and files the restricted-band approvals with nothing forecast against them.

That plan looks less complete than a spreadsheet with every channel filled in. It is also the only one with numbers anyone should believe. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to size the measurement weeks so they produce a result.

Gateway card

### Before you approve the plan

- An objective stated as an observable outcome, with a cost per outcome and a volume
- Expected outcomes by channel, each with its assumption written down
- Flighting with real variation, and a holdout or test on the largest line
- Programmatic lines on inclusion lists, with named sellers
- A reallocation rule for any channel that fails in the first two weeks
- Accounts, tracking and data in the company's name
- Fees stated in dollars

## lowob takeaways

- **Read the promise and the cost basis together.** The conversion assumptions between them are what you are approving.
- **Check where programmatic money goes.** Domain counts, inclusion lists and the seller path, using ads.txt and sellers.json.
- **Ask for the half-budget version.** It shows which channels the planner believes in.
- **Keep measurement and account access verifiable by your company.** The plan ends; the data should stay.

## Common questions

### What should a media plan include?

An objective stated as an observable outcome, the audience, the channel mix with reasons, the flighting, expected results by channel with their assumptions, the measurement approach and, for restricted categories, which channels are open.

### How do you evaluate a media plan?

Interrogate the expected outcomes and the cost basis, ask what the plan looks like at half the budget, check where programmatic money goes, and confirm who owns the accounts and data afterwards.

### What is flighting in a media plan?

The schedule of when each channel runs and at what weight across the plan period. Varying weight deliberately is what lets later analysis tell which channels worked.

### What are ads.txt and sellers.json?

IAB Tech Lab standards. ads.txt lists who a publisher authorises to sell its inventory; sellers.json discloses who each ad system pays under each seller ID. They show the supply path, not whether the ads worked.

## Next move

Before the next plan is approved, ask the planner for two things: the conversion assumption behind each expected-outcome figure, and the same plan at half the budget. Approve nothing whose assumptions nobody can explain.
